A.explanation: A $0.1\,\Omega$ resistor hardly changes the driver current in the $10\,\Omega$ wire, so the potential gradient and the very short balance length stay almost the same.

B.explanation: A $1000\,\Omega$ resistor greatly reduces the current from cell E, greatly reducing the potential gradient along the wire so the $8\,\text{mV}$ balance length becomes a large, precisely measurable fraction of the $1.0\,\text{m}$ wire.

C.explanation: At balance there is zero current in the galvanometer branch between Z and Q, so a $10\,\Omega$ series resistor with the new source causes no potential drop and does not change the balance position.

D.explanation: For the same zero-current reason at null, an $800\,\Omega$ series resistor with the new source does not alter the balance length, so precision is not improved.

hints: Notice the balance condition: at zero galvanometer current the p.d. between P and Z on the resistance wire must equal the new source e.m.f. of about $8\,\text{mV}$.
Calculate the present potential gradient from the $2\,\text{V}$ driver across the $1.0\,\text{m}$, $10\,\Omega$ wire and hence the balance length PZ needed for $8\,\text{mV}$.
Consider how reducing the driver current with a large series resistor changes the volts per metre along the wire and therefore stretches that few-millimetre balance length to tens of centimetres.
walkthrough: This is a potentiometer null method. When the galvanometer reads zero, no current flows in the Z-Q branch, so the p.d. across length PZ of the wire equals the e.m.f. of the source connected between P and Q, about $8\,\text{mV}$.

With cell E alone, the wire current is $I = E/R = 2/10 = 0.20\,\text{A}$. The p.d. across the whole $1.0\,\text{m}$ wire is $2\,\text{V}$, so the potential gradient is $2\,\text{V}$ per $1.0\,\text{m}$.
The balance length is then $l = V/\text{gradient} = 0.008/2 = 0.004\,\text{m} = 4\,\text{mm}$. A few millimetres cannot be located precisely, giving a large percentage uncertainty.

To improve precision the gradient must be made much smaller so the same $8\,\text{mV}$ balances over a much longer length. This is done by lowering the driver current with a large resistor in series with E.

With $1000\,\Omega$ in series, total resistance is about $1010\,\Omega$, so $I \approx 2/1010 \approx 0.0020\,\text{A}$. The p.d. across the wire becomes $I \times 10 \approx 0.020\,\text{V} = 20\,\text{mV}$.

An $8\,\text{mV}$ source then balances at $l \approx 8/20 \times 1.0\,\text{m} \approx 0.40\,\text{m}$, which can be measured with small percentage error. Resistors in the test-source branch carry no current at null and have no effect. This is option B.
